report.source_text: Approximately 1 hour into her hospital course her mother arrived and provided further history. She stated that 24 hours prior to arrival in the ED, the patient was riding a non-motorised scooter around her front yard. The front wheel caught on a lip of the cement and she ran into the garage door, with handle bars turned such that one end of the handle bar contacted the garage door while the other end struck her chest wall. She continued playing and experienced no symptoms other than some mild localised chest wall pain. There was no overlying chest wall deformity, bruising, ecchymosis or haematoma aside from a small left parasternal abrasion noted on physical exam.

report.source_text: In the ED, she denied chest pain, shortness of breath or palpitations and remained haemodynamically stable. She was noted to have multiple runs of stable non-sustained ventricular tachycardia with the longest run lasting approximately 10 s. Intravenous access was established and she was given a normal saline bolus. She was urgently evaluated by paediatric cardiology and paediatric electrophysiology. Her ECG showed frequent ventricular ectopy but were otherwise unremarkable.

report.source_text: She was started on verapamil 40 mg every 8 hours on arrival; on hospital day 3 her dose was increased to 60 mg every 8 hours due to sustained frequent ectopic beats. On day 4, she continued to have premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) but with a decrease in frequency. The paediatric cardiology electrophysiologist evaluated the patient at bedside and cleared her for discharge. She was instructed to continue verapamil at home, to follow-up with paediatric cardiology in 2 weeks and a Holter monitor was ordered. Additionally, she was advised to avoid vigorous physical activity for 4 weeks.

Normal left ventricular size and function, LVEF of 69%; small pericardial effusion with possible pericardial stranding/haematoma (figure 3A); normal right ventricular size with mildly depressed global function and regional wall motion abnormalities as described above. RVEF is 41%.

clinician.trajectory_summary: An 8-year-old girl presented to the ED with lightheadedness and presyncope approximately 24 hours after sustaining blunt chest trauma from a scooter handlebar impact (small left parasternal abrasion noted). EMS rhythm strip demonstrated ventricular tachycardia. On admission, ECG revealed monomorphic accelerated ventricular rhythm with LBBB morphology. Initial workup including troponin I, CBC, CMP, chest radiograph, and transthoracic echocardiogram was unremarkable. Despite normal initial imaging, cardiac MRI obtained on hospital day 2 revealed right ventricular contusion with focal delayed enhancement and edema, regional wall motion abnormalities involving the right ventricular outflow tract and free wall (RVEF 41%), and a subacute precordial hematoma extending across the anterior heart border with small pericardial effusion. The MRI findings correlated with the origin of the ventricular ectopy. The patient was started on verapamil 40mg every 8 hours, increased to 60mg on day 3 for sustained ectopy, with decreased PVC frequency by day 4. She was discharged on verapamil with activity restrictions and cardiology follow-up.
